extracted.intended_audience: graduate students, researchers, and philosophers working in mathematical logic, foundations of mathematics, and constructive/intuitionistic mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic survey of Brouwer's intuitionism and related constructive principles (continuity axioms, choice axioms, bar/fan theorems, Creating Subject, Heyting arithmetic, lawless sequences), explaining their statements, motivations, and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of the Law of Excluded Middle
rubrics_metrics.description: The principle of the excluded middle (A ∨ ¬A) does not hold in intuitionism and in some presentations is taken to be false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text stresses that excluded middle failure is a core distinguishing feature of intuitionism and is the source of many counterexamples and refutations of classical properties of the continuum; it underlies weak counterexample constructions and motivates continuity and choice principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refutation of the Law of Trichotomy
rubrics_metrics.description: The classical law of trichotomy ∀x (x < y ∨ x = y ∨ y < x) is refuted in intuitionism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using continuity/choice-sequence constructions (e.g. real r_α built from a choice sequence α), one obtains ¬∀α (r_α = 0 ∨ r_α ≠ 0), which yields the refutation of trichotomy; continuity axioms therefore deny many classical ordering dichotomies on the continuum.

rubrics_metrics.name: (C-N) Every total real function is continuous
rubrics_metrics.description: C-N: Every total real function is continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Classical counterexamples like the Dirichlet function (0 on rationals, 1 on irrationals) are not legitimate intuitionistic functions because 'being rational' is not a decidable property on the reals. C-N leads to consequences such as non-decomposability of the continuum and rejects certain classical reasoning about functions on reals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neighborhood functions (representation of continuous functionals)
rubrics_metrics.description: A neighborhood function f (representing a continuous functional on sequences) is a function on natural numbers satisfying: (i) for each infinite sequence α there exists n with f(α(overline{n})) > 0, and (ii) ∀n∀m (f(n) > 0 → f(n·m) = f(n)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: f(α(overline{n})) = 0 means initial segment α(overline{n}) is not long enough to compute Φ(α); f(...)=m+1 means that initial segment suffices and Φ(α)=m. Neighborhood functions are a convenient, widely used representation of continuity in the literature (though not used by Brouwer himself).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rephrasing C-N via neighborhood functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Continuity axiom C-N can be rephrased: ∀α∃n A(α,n) → ∃ f ∈ 𝒦 ∀m (f(m) > 0 → ∀β ∈ m A(β,f(m-1))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Here 𝒦 denotes the class of neighborhood functions, and β ∈ m means β's initial segment is coded by m. This formulation captures continuity of operations on Baire space in terms of neighborhood functions and explicit uniformity over initial segments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fan theorem (FAN)
rubrics_metrics.description: FAN: For every fan T, if every branch α ∈ T meets a bar A at some finite stage (∀α ∈ T ∃n A(α(overline{n}))), then there exists a uniform bound m such that every branch meets A by depth ≤ m (∃m ∀α ∈ T ∃n ≤ m A(α(overline{n}))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A fan is a finitely branching spread (tree); FAN expresses a form of compactness classically equivalent to König's lemma. It is a key principle used to recover classical-style theorems like uniform continuity in the intuitionistic setting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequence: Fan theorem implies uniform continuity
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem (FAN): Every continuous real function on a closed interval is uniformly continuous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fan theorem suffices to prove uniform continuity of continuous functions on closed intervals in intuitionistic mathematics; this is one of its main mathematical payoffs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bar principle / Bar theorem (BI)
rubrics_metrics.description: BI (Bar Induction): a schema expressing an induction principle for spreads/trees; one formulation (with decidability subscript D) is given by a (somewhat long) implication asserting that if A is decidable on initial segments and is a bar, and B is closed under certain conditions, then B(ε) holds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BI provides well-foundedness/induction along spreads for decidable predicates; Brouwer's justification uses assumptions about the canonical well-ordering of proofs. BI is classically valid but its intuitionistic justification differs from classical arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bar continuity axiom
rubrics_metrics.description: A combined axiom capturing both continuity and the bar principle (continuity and bar principle sometimes captured in one axiom called the bar continuity axiom).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes continuity and the bar principle can be packaged together; this reflects their close connection in intuitionistic analysis and in justifications of compactness-like principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductively defined neighborhood functions (IK) and K = IK equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Define class 𝒪IK inductively (constants λm.n+1 are in IK; if f(0)=0 and for all x λm.f(x·m) ∈ IK, then f ∈ IK). The statement 𝒦 = 𝒪IK asserts neighborhood functions can be generated inductively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The equality 𝒦 = 𝒪IK is equivalent to BI_D (bar induction for decidable predicates). This ties an inductive generation property of neighborhood functions to bar induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full Axiom of Choice unacceptable (Diaconescu argument)
rubrics_metrics.description: The full Axiom of Choice is unacceptable from a constructive point of view (in the presence of extensionality), because it can be used to derive the Law of Excluded Middle via Diaconescu's construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Diaconescu argument constructs two subsets X and Y of {0,1} depending on an undecided proposition A so that the existence of a choice function on {X,Y} would decide A; thus full AC implies (A ∨ ¬A) and is rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: (AC-N) Countable Choice
rubrics_metrics.description: AC-N (countable choice): ∀R ⊆ ℕ×ℕ (∀m ∃n m R n → ∃α ∈ ℕ^ℕ ∀m m R α(m)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Countable choice is acceptable to many intuitionists; its justification is that a constructive proof of the premise yields a method to choose successive n's step-by-step, building the choice function α explicitly. Semi-intuitionists also accept it.

rubrics_metrics.name: (DC-N) Dependent Choice
rubrics_metrics.description: DC-N (dependent choice): ∀R ⊆ ℕ×ℕ (∀m ∃n m R n → ∀k ∃α ∈ ℕ^ℕ (α(0)=k ∧ ∀i ≥ 0 α(i) R α(i+1))).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent choice is another restricted, constructively acceptable form of choice; classical mathematics also treats choice carefully and attempts to minimize use of full AC, sometimes replacing it with DC where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: (NEP) Numerical Existence Property for Heyting Arithmetic (HA)
rubrics_metrics.description: NEP: If HA ⊢ ∃x A(x) then there exists n ∈ ℕ such that HA ⊢ A( n ).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This property reflects constructivity: existence proofs in HA yield explicit numerals. The text contrasts NEP holding in HA but not in PA, illustrating constructive strength of HA.

rubrics_metrics.name: (MR) Markov's Rule
rubrics_metrics.description: MR: If HA ⊢ ∀x (A(x) ∨ ¬A(x)) and HA ⊢ ¬¬∃x A(x), then HA ⊢ ∃x A(x).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Markov's rule holds in HA (nontrivially) and is applicable for primitive recursive predicates; it is used to relate double-negated existence to actual existence in certain decidable contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: CS1 (Creating Subject: decidability at time n)
rubrics_metrics.description: CS1: □_n A ∨ ¬□_n A — at time n, it can be decided whether the Creating Subject has a proof of A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CS1 formalizes the temporal aspect of the Creating Subject and asserts decidability at each time index for whether a proof is present; the notation □_n A denotes the Creating Subject has a proof of A at time n.

rubrics_metrics.name: CS2 (Creating Subject: persistence of proofs)
rubrics_metrics.description: CS2: □_m A → □_{m+n} A — the Creating Subject never forgets what it has proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This axiom idealizes the Creating Subject by assuming proofs, once obtained, remain available at later times; it formalizes monotonicity of knowledge over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: CS3 (Creating Subject: soundness and provability linked) and CS3+
rubrics_metrics.description: CS3: (∃n □_n A → A) ∧ (A → ¬¬∃n □_n A). CS3+: ∃n □_n A ↔ A (stronger form used by Troelstra).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CS3 asserts the Creating Subject only proves true statements and that truth implies (in a double-negated sense) eventual provability; CS3+ strengthens this to biconditional. The second conjunct of CS3 (A → ¬¬∃n □_n A) is controversial (called the Axiom of Christian Charity) and has been challenged as nonconstructive or inconsistent under some interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axiom of Open Data (for lawless sequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: Axiom of Open Data: For A(α) not containing nonlawlike parameters other than α, A(α) → ∃n ∀β ∈ α(overline{n}) A(β).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This axiom asserts openness of properties of lawless sequences: if A holds of a lawless sequence α, then already some finite initial segment of α forces A to hold for all extensions. It is one of the axioms used in theories of lawless sequences together with strengthened continuity, decidability and density axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Density axiom for lawless sequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Density: every finite sequence is the initial segment of some lawless sequence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Density, together with open-data and other axioms, is part of axiomatizations of lawless sequences; it ensures that finite approximations can be extended to lawless (generic) sequences, and it plays a role in eliminating quantifiers over lawless sequences in the theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kripke's Schema (KS)
rubrics_metrics.description: KS: ∃α (A ↔ ∃n α(n) = 1) — there exists a choice sequence α indicating truth of A by appearance of 1.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KS allows encoding (weak) counterexamples and can express undecidedness via choice sequences. KS, together with continuity axioms, rejects Markov's principle; KS together with Markov's principle implies excluded middle. Kripke showed KS implies existence of nonrecursive functions (published by Kreisel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of nonrecursive functions implied by KS/CS
rubrics_metrics.description: KS (and the Creating Subject axioms CS) imply the existence of nonrecursive functions; explicit constructions show functions f built from □_m predicates or KS cannot be computable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: one can define f(m,n)=0 or 1 depending on □_m(n ∉ X) for a c.e. noncomputable set X; then n ∉ X iff f(m,n)=1 for some m, showing f is noncomputable. This demonstrates that in intuitionism (with these principles) not all functions are computable.
